title: Pyxis Health POC - benchmark triage & routing round-up
summary: Weekly POC sync to triage latency/throughput gaps vs Pyxis's incumbent provider. Reviewed 95th/median latencies, tail events during batching, cold-start behavior, KV/prefix cache effects, and quantization tradeoffs. Agreed next steps: run a deterministic 10k query bench, share full request traces, trial 4-bit quant profile on dedicated slots, and schedule deep SRE session to replicate tail spike. Pricing/commit discussion deferred until stability target is met.
action_items: Sophie Keane; Send trimmed benchmark spreadsheet + cost model by 2026-08-27
Diego Ramos; Run deterministic 10k-query bench with current Pyxis prompt set and attach raw traces; due 2026-08-28
Alex Wu; Provision two dedicated slots with 4-bit quant profile for trial; due 2026-08-30
Jia Chen; Share filtered request/trace logs and example worst-case prompts (PII redacted); due 2026-08-27
Mina Patel; Schedule SRE deep-dive (60m) to reproduce tail spikes with Pyxis team; owner Mina; due 2026-09-01
next_steps: Run determinist 10k bench and compare 50/95/99 percentiles against incumbent baseline
Share raw traces and sample payloads for KV cache investigation
Trial 4-bit quant profile on dedicated slots to assess latency improvements and token quality delta
Schedule SRE deep-dive to repro tail events and discuss routing/fallback playbook
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-25
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Location: Zoom
Notes: recording enabled, live captions on

00:00 Sophie Keane: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you carving the time out. Quick attendance check?
00:08 Dr. Elena Torres: Hi Sophie, Elena here.
00:10 Samir Patel: Samir on for platform.
00:12 Jia Chen: Jia here, SRE.
:14 Lena Ortiz: Lena.
00:16 Sophie Keane: And from our side Diego, Mina, Alex - great. Quick goal for today: triage the benchmark diffs vs the incumbent and align on immediate experiments.
00:29 Diego Ramos: I'll jump in with the bench summary — we ran three buckets: steady-state throughput, cold-start microbursts, and prefix heavy prompts. We compared median, p95, and p99 to the baseline you provided.
00:45 Diego Ramos: For median we look pretty close — within 8 to 12 percent depending on sequence length, so not huge. The big gap is p95 and above during batching at heavy concurrency, where you're seeing tail spikes that match their behavior about 2x ours at p99 for long-context prompts.
01:05 Samir Patel: When you say 'batching at heavy concurrency' are you using continuous batching or fixed windows? We noticed our incumbent uses a 20ms batching window they call batched-slice, which hides some variance.
01:18 Diego Ramos: We're using continuous batching with adaptive windows; we do prioritize latency SLOs, so we sometimes flush earlier. That behavior can create tail variance when a lot of long sequences arrive together.
01:30 Jia Chen: The baseline reported lower p99, I guess they may be sacrificing median to smooth the tail?
01:36 Diego Ramos: Exactly, could be an intentional trade. Also their runtime has a KV cache pre-warmed layer for commonly seen prefixes, which reduces long-tail for repeat prompts.
01:49 Lena Ortiz: We do have a lot of repeated intents with similar prefixes in the triage data. How big of an impact is prefix caching?
01:56 Alex Wu: In our lab cases, enabling prefix/KV cache cut end-to-end token generation latency by about 18-22 percent for those heavy prefix flows, sometimes more if the prefix is large and reused frequently. But it increases memory footprint and control plane complexity.
02:12 Dr. Elena Torres: Does that explain the p99 difference or is it mostly batching?
02:17 Diego Ramos: Both. The p99 delta looks like a combination: when a heavy prefix hits during a microburst, you get compounding queuing + long decode times. If prefix cache is warm those decodes are shorter.
02:30 Samir Patel: What about quantization? Our incumbent claims 4-bit quant at scale — have you tried comparable quant profiles?
02:37 Diego Ramos: We've been cautious in the POC — we've run 8-bit and mixed int8/16 profiles. The 4-bit path is available but we want to validate quality first. 4-bit gives latency gains and reduces GPU memory allowing higher batching but sometimes increases perplexity and rare-case hallucination.
02:55 Dr. Elena Torres: For us model quality is paramount for safety-critical suggestions, so any quality delta needs to be measured against our eval set.
03:03 Mina Patel: Totally. We suggested earlier running quant A/Bs with your eval prompts. The plan today is to propose a 4-bit trial on a dedicated slot so we isolate variables.
03:14 Sophie Keane: Diego, can you walk through the deterministic bench plan you propose?
03:18 Diego Ramos: Sure — we'll use the canonical Pyxis prompt set you shared, 10k deterministic queries across length buckets (short, medium, long), fixed inter-arrival times to remove burstiness initially, then a microburst phase to simulate concurrency. We'll collect token-level traces, batch sizes, wait times, and GPU utilization.
03:34 Samir Patel: How do you guarantee determinism? Last time our reported numbers had noise from autoscaling decisions.
03:39 Diego Ramos: We'll pin to dedicated slots for the run and disable autoscaling. Also we will run multiple iterations and take the median across runs.
03:47 Jia Chen: Please include the raw traces, not just the aggregated numbers — we need to see the queuing moments and kernel-level timestamps to map to our logs.
03:55 Diego Ramos: Yep we'll attach the raw traces CSV.
04:02 Lena Ortiz: I also want clarity on the routing/fallback story — we've seen the incumbent route to smaller model variants when latencies climb, which keeps p95 low at the cost of occasional quality change. What's Redwood's fallback behavior?
04:16 Diego Ramos: We have routing policies — latency-first, cost-first, and quality-preserving. For this POC we recommend a canary fallback to a semantically equivalent but faster quantized variant with similarity checks and a safety fallback to the original if the similarity drops. But that introduces complexity in validation.
04:35 Dr. Elena Torres: That sounds reasonable if similarity checks are strict. We cannot accept silent degradation.
04:41 Diego Ramos: Agree — similarity thresholds should be tuned to your eval set.
04:45 Mina Patel: Quick note: we observed two classes of tail spikes in today's logs — 1) cold-cache warm-up phase and 2) concurrency compaction where lots of long sequences queue behind one long decode. The remediation for (1) is prewarm/prefix caching; for (2) is shaping and routing (route long sequences to dedicated lanes or cap batch sizes).
05:10 Samir Patel: Can you simulate the incumbent's smoothing behavior (20ms fixed window) so we have an apples-to-apples?
05:17 Diego Ramos: Yes we can run a variant with a fixed flush window and measure median vs p95 tradeoffs. We'll include that in the bench plan.
05:24 Jia Chen: Are there any network-level issues? We saw occasional host-to-host spikes that line up with our infra maintenance windows.
05:30 Alex Wu: We looked at network — very little variance on our side in the lab. Most spikes reproduced in pure local bench runs, so it's likely runtime-scheduling + batching interactions rather than cloud network.
05:44 Lena Ortiz: On the quality front, do you have a way to flag responses where quantization caused divergence?
05:50 Diego Ramos: We'll run a diff metric against your eval judgments and flag responses where semantic similarity drops below the threshold. We can export those items as part of the bench artifact.
05:59 Samir Patel: About cost — if we go to dedicated slots with 4-bit we expect unit cost changes, right? We need that modeled before commiting.
06:06 Sophie Keane: We'll include a cost model comparing host vs dedicated with quantization assumptions in the spreadsheet Sophie will send. That will show per-1M token cost across options.
06:17 Dr. Elena Torres: Okay, so to recap: Diego runs the deterministic 10k bench with variants (continuous batching, fixed-window 20ms, prefix-cache on/off, and a 4-bit trial on isolated slot) and shares traces; Alex provisions the slots; Jia shares logs; Sophie sends spreadsheet and cost model. We schedule deep SRE dive if bench reproduces the p99 gap.
06:36 Diego Ramos: Correct. Also we'll capture per-request batch size histograms and token decode time distributions.
06:44 Mina Patel: I'll follow up with calendar invites for the deep dive and next sync.
06:48 Lena Ortiz: One ask — can you annotate the benchmark outputs with example prompts that fall in the p99? That helps our product team prioritize.
06:55 Diego Ramos: Yes we'll add top-k offending prompts and examples.
06:59 Samir Patel: Timeline check — can the bench and artifacts come by Friday? (2026-08-28)
07:04 Diego Ramos: We'll aim for Friday. If anything slips we'll flag.
07:08 Sophie Keane: Great — any final questions?
07:10 Dr. Elena Torres: Not from me. Appreciate the focused triage.
07:12 Lena Ortiz: Thanks all.
07:15 Sophie Keane: Thanks everyone, end of call.
